Order planning

Understanding minimum order quantities

FORME Packaging editorialUpdated October 21, 20263 min read

A minimum order is usually tied to a particular custom specification. Discuss the quantity for each size, artwork version and material combination before finalizing your range.

In this guideWhy minimums vary between projectsPlan a range without unnecessary variantsUse samples to reduce uncertaintyThink through storage and reordersDiscuss your packaging →

Why minimums vary between projects

Material procurement, printing setup, cutting tools, finishing and assembly all affect how a custom order is planned. A straightforward printed mailer and a multi-compartment rigid gift set need different operations. There is no single minimum that can describe every format on this site.

Ask whether the minimum applies to a structure, a size, a printed design or a total order. Several products sharing a similar appearance do not automatically share the same tooling. A few millimeters of dimensional change may still require a revised cutting layout or insert.

Plan a range without unnecessary variants

List the products that could share a common outer size. A different insert or printed sleeve may allow a coordinated range, but only if the fit and assembly remain practical. Avoid leaving a small item loose inside a large box solely to combine quantities.

Separate essential differences from optional ones. You might need two different insert layouts but only one exterior artwork version. Ask for the cost and minimum of each alternative so the decision is based on the complete pack rather than a unit figure alone.

Use samples to reduce uncertainty

A structural sample checks the shape and fit; a decorated sample also addresses paper, color and finishing. Confirm which sample you are ordering and which production features it represents. A digital mockup is useful for artwork placement but cannot demonstrate closure resistance or the way a bottle sits in its insert.

Before requesting a short trial, explain whether you are testing a new product, preparing a launch or replacing existing packaging. That context helps the supplier propose a realistic sampling and production route.

Think through storage and reorders

  • Expected usage by month and by product size.
  • Storage space for flat or assembled packaging.
  • Artwork changes likely before the next order.
  • Material references and approved sample retained for reorders.
  • Target delivery date and the time needed for approval.

Order volume should fit both demand and storage. Request a written quotation for your likely quantities and confirm the reorder specification rather than assuming the first order terms remain unchanged.
